extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, and researchers of news production
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying the unwritten rules and practical standards journalists use to decide which events become news and how stories are produced within news organizations. Emphasizes availability, suitability, organizational roles, and external pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Determines the availability of news and relates journalists to sources; information must be accessible before it can become news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability depends on access between sources and journalists, which is differentially distributed and shaped by social distance and power. Economically and politically powerful actors gain easier access; those lacking power are harder to reach and usually enter the news only when producing disorder. Journalists usually have more available information than they can use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments that winnow available information to what is feasible and appropriate to cover for the intended audience within limited staff, time, and space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suitability ties journalists to audiences and determines what can be covered given deadline and resource constraints. It requires quick methods of empirical inquiry, often produces primarily descriptive reporting, and involves weighing one story against others (relational/comparable judgments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Source considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria related to the characteristics of sources (who provides information) that affect story selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sources include actors observed or interviewed and those who supply background or suggestions; salient is that sources act as representatives of organized/unorganized interests. Their power, ability to preschedule events, and access to journalists are crucial. Sources are also often part of the audience (especially in Washington).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments about the substantive content or significance of a potential story (one of the seven sets of considerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as one of the principal sets of considerations (alongside source, product, value, commercial, audience, and political). These concern the inherent newsworthiness or importance of the subject matter and will be unpacked in later chapters (here presented as a distinct class of considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations that treat news as a product to be manufactured and tailored for markets and formats (one of the seven sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encompasses constraints and standards tied to the medium (television vs. magazine), format decisions (length, order), and the assembly-line nature of production where stories are assembled from many parts under deadline conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations tied to values (professional or cultural) that guide what journalists deem appropriate to report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguished from 'norms' or 'values' in the analytic sense here, but acknowledged as a set of considerations that interact with other factors (they are one of seven sets and overlap with other considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Market and firm-level economic pressures and imperatives that influence story selection (one of the seven sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations are part of profit-seeking firms; commercial pressures can push towards sensationalism when economic indicators fall, but when firms are prosperous journalists may resist overtly commercializing content. Commercial considerations can be imposed from beyond the newsroom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria based on audience interests, habits, and the audience's role as consumer that affect story choice (one of the seven sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The audience is not merely a recipient but a source of income whose viewing/reading behavior partially affects journalists' source choices; notionally captured by 'we get the news we deserve' but the author argues audiences are not directly involved in choosing news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: External political pressures and ideological alignments that constrain or shape story selection (one of the seven sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes pressure from political actors, possible alignment with dominant ideologies (often unconscious), and political forces that may cause journalists to alter selection especially when faced with threats or consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick applicability / reliance on 'feel' (intuitive judgments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations must be rapidly and easily applicable so journalists can make swift, often intuitive, decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the volume of daily choices and deadlines, journalists act on quick, virtually intuitive judgments (referred to as 'feel'). Considerations therefore favor simple heuristics to avoid excessive deliberation and uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations must be adaptable to the endless variety of available news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although easily applied, considerations must also be flexible so they can be reinterpreted across different contexts and types of events; they are not rigid rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relational and comparable judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Suitability of one story depends on other available stories; considerations must allow comparison across alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because news space/time is limited, editors compare candidate stories relative to one another; considerations therefore need to be relational so editors can choose among competing items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusionary and exclusionary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate types of considerations used to add stories to or drop stories from the news list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists apply inclusionary criteria (reasons to add) and exclusionary criteria (reasons to drop) during the ongoing selection process; both function under time pressure and changing availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Easily rationalized decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions should be defensible with an acceptable rationale if a story is replaced or altered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations are designed so replacements or drops can be explained post hoc; editors prefer reasons that can be readily articulated to justify choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection and production considerations are driven by efficiency: supply suitable news with minimal time, effort, and cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of limited resources, considerations prioritize methods and story choices that minimize staff/time/expenditure while maintaining necessary supply of news; economic constraints therefore shape journalistic practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus and hierarchical enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of considerations requires agreement among journalists and is reinforced by newsroom hierarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent chaos given many overlapping considerations, news judgment depends on consensus and a hierarchical organization where higher-power actors (top editors/producers) can enforce which considerations are relevant for a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routinization of story selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection must be routinized (formalized into predictable processes) so journalists can manage enormous potential choice sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because journalists cannot re-decide selection from scratch each day, they create routines/conventions to make the task manageable; these routines are embedded in organizational structures and roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipated stories / prescheduled events as a resource
rubrics_metrics.description: Planned events (press conferences, hearings, ceremonies) provide predictable, schedulable stories that ease staffing and access concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipated stories guarantee access, allow scheduling of crews/reporters, and reduce fear of 'not having enough news.' Sources may preschedule events to gain coverage; not all anticipated stories are suitable but they form a major portion of supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wire services and beats for story suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire services and reporters' beats are primary suppliers of story suggestions which initiate the selection process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wire services spin out continuous story leads; reporters are evaluated on their ability to suggest suitable stories. Top editors often begin weekly meetings by mining reporters' social interactions for ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story design and continuous review (queries and producers)
rubrics_metrics.description: After selection, stories are designed (queries drafted) and remain under continuous review; stories can be killed or postponed based on feasibility and timeliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associate producers or writers draft queries outlining themes and questions; top/senior editors contribute. Stories may be killed if information is not available in time, require too much rewriting, become stale, or are displaced by newer items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual checking and the role of researchers (checkers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal factual verification by researchers/checkers who can override writers/editors on demonstrable factual errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checkers (often lower in hierarchy) have formal authority to stop publication if they can provide convincing evidence of factual inaccuracies; they generally cannot overturn non-factual assumptions or generalizations. Reporters also participate in checking and approving copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadline constraints shaping method and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Immutable deadlines (especially in television) constrain the depth of reporting methods and favor descriptive over analytical work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deadlines limit time and staff available, forcing use of quickly applied empirical methods and restricting the number of findings presented. This distinguishes routine journalism from in-depth social science analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access reflects social structure and power
rubrics_metrics.description: Who gets access to journalists is a function of social and power hierarchies outside the newsroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because access maps onto social structure (economic/political power), coverage is hierarchically distributed. Journalists' available information is therefore biased toward powerful sectors unless disruptive events force attention to less powerful actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational division of labor and formal roles in selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal newsroom roles (policy makers, top editors/producers, section heads, reporters, researchers) determine who suggests, selects, designs, produces, and approves stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top editors/producers have final authority over content, length, and order; section heads ready stories; reporters suggest and gather info; researchers check facts. The assembly-line (seriatim) process implies multiple hands in each story's pathway, affecting selection and production decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources' capacity to create 'public events' and gain access
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups powerful enough can create events designed to attract media attention and thus influence what becomes news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some actors manufacture newsworthy events (media events), schedule them to fit newsroom routines, and supply advance information to make their stories more likely to be judged available and suitable.
